items.title: Bill Ackman Outlines The Activist Playbook To Reinstate Jensen Huang | Silicon Valley & The World
items.summary: At Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, billionaire activist investor Bill Ackman outlined how he would theoretically run a campaign to reinstate ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang—though he noted his direct involvement is "unlikely."
items.content_text:
## TL;DR
At Semafor’s *Silicon Valley & The World*, billionaire activist investor Bill Ackman outlined how he would theoretically run a campaign to reinstate ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang—though he noted his direct involvement is "unlikely." Alongside the President’s chief technology advisor (referred to as "Director"), Ackman also discussed the rise of founder-controlled public companies, U.S. AI export controls, and how commercial instincts and AI are reshaping scientific philanthropy.

## The Activist Playbook for Reinstating Jensen Huang
* **Ackman’s Defense:** Bill Ackman rushed to Huang’s defense out of a belief in "innocent until proven guilty" and a favorable past relationship with Huang, noting that the best time to help someone is when they are down.
* **Likelihood of Involvement:** Ackman said it is "unlikely" he will get directly involved, though he called it a "pretty interesting activist setup" with "Steve Jobsian" elements that would likely garner significant shareholder support.
* **Tactical Execution:** 
  * Establish the facts first to resolve current legal uncertainties; if Huang’s missteps were a "personal foible as opposed to a corporate defense conspiracy," there is a strong case for reinstatement.
  * Partner with Huang, who owns 3% of Nvidia, to call a special shareholder meeting.
  * Present the facts and propose board changes—Ackman expects "the writing will be on the wall very quickly," forcing the board to reinstate Huang before a vote even occurs.
* **Board Ethics on Lying:** While "truth is pretty darn important" between a board and a CEO, Ackman distinguished between a lie regarding a personal relationship versus a lie about next quarter's revenue or core business operations.

## Founder Control & Public Market Short-Termism
* **The Rise of the "Golden Share":** Moderator Liz Hoffman noted that Anthropic is going public this week with a structure giving its seven cofounders a "golden share" that controls nearly everything at the company.
* **The Case for Founder Control:** Ackman argued that founder-led companies historically create far more long-term value than dispersed-ownership companies run by hired CEOs, though he cautioned against blindly passing that golden share to the "next generation."
* **Wall Street Short-Termism:** 
  * Index funds—which Ackman described as automated, passive entities operating for basis points rather than "real owners"—now own 25% of corporate America.
  * Combined with quantitative trading, options, and 3x levered ETFs, public markets force short-term thinking, making founder control or large, long-term anchor investors increasingly logical.

## U.S. Tech Stack, Export Controls & Security
* **Exporting the U.S. Stack:** The Director emphasized that winning in superintelligence (SI) requires U.S. companies to have the chips they need, while also sharing a trusted Western tech stack globally via the **American SI Export Program** (created by executive order in July of last year).
* **Chip Diversion & Enforcement:** Addressing tensions over Nvidia's chip sales, the Director pointed to new Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) rules announced today regarding remote chip access and licensing requirements for certain countries.
* **Workforce & IP Security:** With young AI companies growing rapidly, the Director urged CEOs to take security seriously and protect frontier model weights—calling them some of the most valuable assets in the world.

## AI in Science & Reforming Philanthropy
* **Ackman’s AI-Native Brain Institute:** Ackman and his wife are endowing a Brain Institute in New York (initially $400M, now closer to $800M). Operating in "super-founder mode," Ackman’s first hires include a Chief AI Officer, and he previously connected Huang’s healthcare team with Mount Sinai’s brain data.
* **Free Market Over Mandates:** Both Ackman and the Director rejected the idea of forcing AI labs to devote 25% of their compute to curing cancer or brain disease.
* **SI for Science Momentum:** 
  * The Director highlighted that philanthropic organizations like the Chan Zuckerberg Biohub and Patrick Collison’s Arc Institute are investing hundreds of millions to billions into SI-powered science.
  * A month ago, the administration hosted an "SI for Science" event announcing **$2.4 billion** in donations from the SI community to provide free compute to American scientists.
  * Roughly a quarter of OpenAI (nearly a quarter of a trillion dollars) and similar commitments from Anthropic's founders are earmarked for philanthropic endeavors.
* **Applying Commercial Instincts to Nonprofits:** 
  * Having given away **$1.5 billion** over 20 years through the Pershing Square Foundation, Ackman criticized traditional philanthropy for enormous waste, lack of M&A, and lack of equity compensation.
  * His Brain Institute will operate with commercial instincts: creating and monetizing IP through company formation, sharing equity with employees, and utilizing a captive venture fund (which has already invested **$90 million** in brain-computer interface and device companies) to funnel returns back into the institute.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **On Nvidia Governance:** If an activist partners with Jensen Huang (3% owner) to call a special meeting, "the writing will be on the wall very quickly... at which point you don't even have to go to the meeting, you just put him back in." — *Bill Ackman*
* **On Scientific Discovery:** "SI is going to transform entirely the way that scientists do their work from material science, to chemistry, to math, to physics, to biochemistry, to the way the pharmaceuticals are developed." — *Director (President's Chief Technology Advisor)*
* **On Philanthropic Capital:** "There's going to be more money moving into the SI for Science field than we could ever imagine." — *Director (President's Chief Technology Advisor)*

## Notable Quotes
> "If it's a personal foible as opposed to a corporate defense conspiracy, I think there's a very powerful case for putting him back in place." — *Bill Ackman, on Jensen Huang*

> "More and more of American companies are being controlled by automated machines that operate for basis points and own 25% of corporate America... it's not a world in which owners behave like owners, except for a very small handful of more active owners and founders." — *Bill Ackman*

> "You don't have to be an expert in this to understand how important the weights are to these frontier models. These are some of the most important and most valuable assets in the entire world, and they should be rightfully protected." — *Director (President's Chief Technology Advisor)*

> "People have created a lot more value for the world with for-profit companies than they have with nonprofits, but there are gaps in the capital markets where nonprofits can step in and accomplish things." — *Bill Ackman*

items.title: Dylan Patel, SemiAnalysis
items.summary: Dylan Patel is expanding SemiAnalysis into a research and investment empire—spanning 115 employees, the acquisition of Citrini Research, and a new $500 million hardware-focused venture fund—while tracking major shifts in AI, including multi-gigawatt data center permitting delays and a market transition where product execution (like Meta’s Muse and Perplexity) is outperforming raw foundation model labs.
items.content_text:
**TL;DR**
Dylan Patel is expanding SemiAnalysis into a research and investment empire—spanning 115 employees, the acquisition of Citrini Research, and a new $500 million hardware-focused venture fund—while tracking major shifts in AI, including multi-gigawatt data center permitting delays and a market transition where product execution (like Meta’s Muse and Perplexity) is outperforming raw foundation model labs.

## Data Center Bottlenecks, Regulation & Public Perception
* **Permitting Delays Over Supply Chain:** SemiAnalysis has pushed back multiple gigawatts of data center capacity from 2027 into 2028, and pushed several gigawatts out of 2028 entirely—not due to labor or equipment shortages, but because permits are unavailable.
* **Texas Regulatory Landscape:** Governor Hinojosa in Texas has been constructive, signaling she will not stop data centers as long as they do not raise electricity prices and are reasonable stewards of water.
  * However, she holds significant leverage via water, wastewater, stormwater, and air permits (which can even stop off-grid data centers).
  * A potential sticking point is union labor mandates, as Texas has very little union labor and non-union electricians and industrial plumbers on data center sites already make $200,000+ per year.
* **Public Ignorance vs. Sentiment:** A poll conducted by SemiAnalysis and David Shor across counties with 100MW+ data centers revealed that **49%** of residents did not even know a data center was in their county. In counties with a 100MW+ data center planned in the next three years, only **40%** knew it was coming.
  * Most local opposition stems from nebulous anti-AI sentiment online rather than actual local impact, though poorly executed projects can be loud or fail to return tax value.
  * Conversely, well-structured projects generate massive local revenue—such as a county in Louisiana that paid all its teachers $20,000 bonuses from data center property taxes. Patel notes companies can easily buy goodwill by subsidizing power for everyone within a 30-mile radius.
* **The Water Usage Myth:** Patel debunked exaggerated water narratives (citing a *New York Times* bestseller that overestimated data center water usage by 1,000x), noting that all of Elon Musk’s data centers use less embedded water than **three In-N-Out** restaurants when accounting for the agricultural supply chain of beef versus chip fabs and power generation.

## The AI Race: Models vs. Products
* **Lab Competition:** Responding to host Molly O'Shea’s framing of the "Four Seasons of AI" (Google, Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceX), Patel noted that markets smooth out valuations rather than swinging wildly on single releases. Anthropic dominated Q2, OpenAI dominated Q3, and Anthropic is back ahead with Opus 3.5 and Fable 5.2 while OpenAI delays model releases.
* **Product Execution Beats Raw Models:** Patel argued that OpenAI and Anthropic are bad at building products. Meta’s **Muse** (beta-tested by Patel) and **Instinct** (which primarily uses open models) are vastly superior products compared to OpenAI’s **Dots** or Codex, which are crippled by overzealous safety filters ("Guardian"). He also criticized OpenAI’s chat app UI as confusing for a billion-user app.
* **SemiAnalysis’s $15M AI Spend:** SemiAnalysis spends **$15 million per year** on AI. Over the last few months, its spend on persistent agents jumped from 0% to **45%**—with the vast majority flowing through **Perplexity** (which acts as a better harness over Claude and OpenAI on the backend) rather than Anthropic’s Claude tags or OpenAI’s Dots.
* **Enterprise Stickiness & Startup Viability:** While developer tools like CloudCode and Codex are easy to switch away from, enterprise contracts are becoming sticky (e.g., Anthropic offering discounts if **70%+** of an enterprise's AI spend is with them). Among application startups, Patel believes most will fail, though **Instinct**, **Sierra**, and **Harvey** are showing real revenue growth and staying power (even as Harvey’s margins seesaw).

## Building the SemiAnalysis Empire & $500M VC Fund
* **Global Footprint & Business Model:** SemiAnalysis now employs **115 people** across **15 countries** (with offices in New York, Chicago, SF, Oregon, Singapore, and Korea). Its core revenue comes from selling proprietary datasets (tracking every data center, chip, and supply chain metric globally) and one-on-one consulting for hyperscalers, semiconductor firms, and AI labs.
* **Acquiring Citrini Research:** Patel acquired Citrini Research (led by James and director of research Kyle) to help operationalize their business. Citrini remains a completely separate company with full editorial independence—even when their macro/AI calls turn bearish, contrasting with Patel’s long-term bullishness.
* **$500M Solo GP Venture Fund:** Patel raised a **$500 million** early-stage (Seed/Series A) venture fund as a solo GP, focusing on hardware, infrastructure, silicon, optics, manufacturing, networking, and robotics—areas where SemiAnalysis’s deep technical bench (former ASML, TSMC, Intel, Nvidia, and hyperscaler engineers) gives him an edge.
* **Strict Independence & Firewalls:** The fund is legally firewalled from SemiAnalysis and Citrini. Patel refuses to take paid partnerships or ads, and maintains strict objectivity—publicly criticizing his biggest customers (e.g., calling out Nvidia’s anti-competitive practices with neoclouds) and even his own portfolio companies (e.g., publicly noting Fluidstack’s data center delays, or critiquing Iris Energy/IREN’s unreliable cloud tech while acknowledging the value of their powered land).

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **Space Data Centers:** Engineering data centers in space is extremely difficult and will not solve capacity constraints in the next 3–4 years. While Elon Musk is aiming for 2028, Patel "takes the over" on that timeline, predicting **1 gigawatt in space** sometime this decade (around **2030**) — *Dylan Patel*.
* **Hardware Innovation Acceleration:** Within **1 year**, the number of companies building hardware—and doing it well—will skyrocket, driven by AI models improving on complex technical benchmarks like SemiAnalysis’s new **GDPX** (which tests cyber, chip design, hardware design, material science, bio, and quant RSI) — *Dylan Patel*.
* **Startup Attrition:** Most AI application startups will fail, though select companies with strong product-market fit and revenue velocity (such as Instinct, Sierra, and Harvey) will achieve long-term staying power — *Dylan Patel*.

## Notable Quotes
> "49% of people in counties that have a 100-megawatt data center did not even know there was a data center in their county." — Dylan Patel

> "All of Elon Musk's data centers use less water than three In-N-Outs... if you count the supply chain of cows." — Dylan Patel

> "Over the last few months, we've gone from zero persistent agents to 45% of our $15 million a year AI spend being persistent agents. And that 45%, the vast majority of it is not through Anthropic's Claude tags or OpenAI's Slack agent or Dots... it's through Perplexity." — Dylan Patel

> "Just because you're invested in something, or you have financial interest, doesn't mean you have to just be the tail that's wagged by the dog." — Dylan Patel

items.title: Giving Every Kid a Stake in Capitalism | Brad Gerstner & Geoffrey Canada
items.summary: Passed on July 4, 2025, the Invest America Act automatically opens universal capital accounts (530A / "Trump accounts") for every American child—70 million accounts are already open—seeding $1,000 in the S&P 500 at birth and unlocking a "Giving Pledge 2.0" wave of direct philanthropy from donors like Michael Dell and Elon Musk.
items.content_text:
## TL;DR
Passed on July 4, 2025, the Invest America Act automatically opens universal capital accounts (530A / "Trump accounts") for every American child—70 million accounts are already open—seeding $1,000 in the S&P 500 at birth and unlocking a "Giving Pledge 2.0" wave of direct philanthropy from donors like Michael Dell and Elon Musk. Brad Gerstner and Geoffrey Canada argue that giving every kid a stake in capitalism is the essential social contract for the AI age, solving the distribution problem that education alone cannot fix.

## The Capital Gap & Social Unrest
*   **Education Isn't Enough Without Capital:** Geoffrey Canada (Founder, Harlem Children's Zone) noted that despite graduating over 2,000 kids with college degrees (with ~1,000 currently in college), a single $500–$1,500 emergency can still bankrupt them.
    *   Earlier efforts like the 2009 Seed program and HCZ CEO Kwame Osei-Kessy's 2021 "Wealth Build" initiative (which raised over $100 million) proved the concept, but lacked national scale.
*   **The Ticking Time Bomb:** Canada warned that when parents sacrifice their health and their kids still fall behind, the system breeds revolt—citing 1960s riots, Raj Chetty's research on the fading American Dream, and modern protests in London, Paris, and Spain (4 million protesters).
    *   He emphasized this is not just an inner-city issue, but an economic crisis affecting poor white communities just as deeply.
*   **Capitalism Without Capital:** Brad Gerstner (Founder & CEO, Altimeter Capital) pointed out that less than half of Americans under age 40 believe in capitalism simply because they have no capital.

## How Invest America (530A) Accounts Work
*   **Automatic & Universal:** Signed into law on July 4, 2025, the Treasury Department automatically opens a 530A account for all 3.7 million babies born annually (10,000 per day) with $1,000 invested in the S&P 500.
    *   Every American child under 18 was grandfathered in, resulting in 70 million accounts already open.
*   **Product Design & Ownership:** Parents simply download an app to claim the account; there is no cash and no investment decisions, as all funds sweep automatically into the S&P 500.
    *   To make compounding tangible, the app displays look-through ownership of underlying companies like Apple, Berkshire Hathaway, and Walmart, and includes an easy QR code/Apple Pay button for $5–$10 contributions.
    *   At age 18, recipients can withdraw up to 25% for a home, business, college, or trade, while the remainder rolls into an IRA.
*   **Economic Impact:** A Milken Institute study by Rob Shapiro and Kevin Hassett found universal capital accounts increase high school/college graduation, homeownership, business creation, and taxpaying rates, while reducing incarceration.

## Giving Pledge 2.0: Direct Philanthropy at Scale
*   **Eliminating Friction:** Patrick O'Shaughnessy highlighted that the original Giving Pledge lacked tangible, direct impact. The new accounts create a direct-giving platform via a one-page agreement with the U.S. Treasury.
*   **Major Commitments:**
    *   **Michael & Susan Dell:** Contributed $6.25 billion ($250 each to 25 million kids aged 2–10 in the bottom 75% of zip codes).
    *   **Elon Musk & SpaceX:** Musk pledged 1 share of SpaceX to all 70 million kids (an $11.5 billion gift), while SpaceX CEO Gwynne Shotwell is giving 2 million shares to kids aged 10–18 in the bottom 50% of income zip codes.
    *   **Regional & Corporate Donors:** Gerstner funded $250 for every child under 5 in Indiana's bottom zip codes and $250 each for 3,000 kids at a Bronx school; Ray Dalio (CT), Frank Slootman (MT), and Neal Mehta ($100 per kid in San Francisco) have joined, and Anthropic announced its philanthropic arm will fund direct citizen accounts.

## Overcoming Diffusion, Political, & Education Hurdles
*   **The "Free Money" Scam Perception:** Canada stressed that poor families often assume free money is a scam. HCZ, Robin Hood, and NYC teachers will push parents to claim accounts on the first day of kindergarten.
*   **Bipartisan Politics & Branding:** While the "Trump accounts" moniker alienates some Democrats—similar to early GOP resistance to "Obamacare"—the policy has broad bipartisan backing (including Presidents Clinton and Obama, Governors Gavin Newsom and Wes Moore, Senator Cory Booker, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent).
    *   Account creation is permanent, though the $1,000 birth grant is funded through 2029 and requires Congressional reauthorization every four years.
    *   Gerstner urged Newsom to block-grant California's $200 million Cal Kids program directly into 530A accounts to consolidate fragmented state efforts.
*   **Financial Literacy:** HCZ acquired an ed-tech company to teach parents and kids about compounding. Texas has already deployed a curriculum around these accounts for 500,000 students, 38 states mandate financial literacy, and AI tutors (via OpenAI/Anthropic) will be embedded directly in the app.

## AI, Keynes's Forecast, & The New Social Contract
*   **Sharing AI's Upside:** Canada noted that young people mostly hear that AI will eliminate their jobs or pose existential risks; giving them equity in companies like SpaceX, OpenAI, and Anthropic ensures they share in the reward, not just the risk.
*   **Keynes's 1930 Parallel:** Gerstner cited John Maynard Keynes's 1930 essay *"Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren"*—written during 22% unemployment (vs. 4.1% today)—which coined "technological unemployment" and predicted living standards would rise 4x–8x in 100 years (by 2030, the economy is 8.2x larger, and 80% of today's jobs didn't exist in 1930).
*   **1935 vs. 2025:** Just as the 1935 Social Security Act created a social contract for the industrial age to protect *labor*, the 2025 Invest America Act creates the social contract for the AI age by giving every citizen *capital*.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
*   "In just a few months, every one of those [70 million] accounts will have money in it." — Brad Gerstner
*   "Over the next 10 to 15 years, we will have $3 to $5 trillion dollars in these accounts." — Brad Gerstner
*   "The $25 trillion dollars of wealth in the United States that's going to change hands over the course of the next 10 to 15 years, you're going to see 10 or 20% of that go directly into these kids' accounts." — Brad Gerstner
*   "I'm highly confident that [making the $1,000 at birth permanent] will get done. I think that could even get done in this lame duck session." — Brad Gerstner

## Notable Quotes
> "There is no capitalism without capital." — Brad Gerstner

> "You can have a great education. You have no money. You are literally one emergency away from bankruptcy." — Geoffrey Canada

> "We do not have an abundance problem. We do not have an invention problem. We have a distribution problem." — Brad Gerstner

> "I wasn't down with capitalism until I got some capital." — Geoffrey Canada

items.title: How One Piece Of Advice Helped Remitly’s Founder Build A $4.6 Billion FinTech Giant
items.summary: A single piece of advice from Harvard Business School professor Nittin Noria—to take "the road less traveled" by leaving Barkley's London headquarters for Nairobi, Kenya—led Matt Oppenheimer to discover the broken cross-border payments system and build Remitly into a $4.6 billion FinTech giant processing $75 billion annually across 175+ countries.
items.content_text:
**TL;DR:** A single piece of advice from Harvard Business School professor Nittin Noria—to take "the road less traveled" by leaving Barkley's London headquarters for Nairobi, Kenya—led Matt Oppenheimer to discover the broken cross-border payments system and build Remitly into a $4.6 billion FinTech giant processing $75 billion annually across 175+ countries.

## The Advice That Sparked Remitly
* **The Mentor:** Nittin Noria, Oppenheimer's professor in Harvard Business School's *Authentic Leadership Development* class (originally started by Bill George) and later Dean of HBS, gave Oppenheimer career-altering advice after business school.
* **The Road Less Traveled:** When Oppenheimer accepted a global leadership role at Barkley's Bank in London (One Churchill Place), Noria warned him that everyone would advise against leaving headquarters for his second rotation—and urged him to go to Nairobi, Kenya instead to gain a truly global perspective.
* **Discovering the Problem:** In Nairobi, Oppenheimer was the only North American expat on Barkley's consumer leadership team. Living in Kenyan shillings while paid in British pounds—and watching local friends like Fiona rely on a sister's Bank of America debit card for basic living expenses—exposed how expensive, slow, and inconvenient cross-border financial services were.

## Scaling Through Intense Short-Term Focus
* **Current Scale:** Remitly now has a ~$4.6 billion market cap, processes $75 billion+ in annual transfers across 175+ countries, reaches 5 billion+ bank accounts and hundreds of thousands of cash pickup locations, and delivers 90%+ of transactions in under an hour.
* **Disciplined Corridor Rollout:** Founded in 2011, Remitly tackled state-by-state regulation and working capital complexity by focusing exclusively on US (specifically Washington state) to the Philippines—a ~$10 billion annual volume corridor at the time—for its first two years, before adding India in year three and Mexico in year four.
  * *Trade-off:* This narrow focus initially made fundraising harder, as VCs questioned whether Remitly could replicate its model in new countries, but Oppenheimer credits it with enabling intentional, customer-centric growth without sacrificing trust.
* **Customer-Centric Testing Programs:**
  * **Remitly Travel:** Reimburses employees who travel to Remitly's operating countries and use the platform to send money, surfacing real-world friction points like cash-pickup delays or Know Your Customer (KYC) issues.
  * **Remitly Scholars:** Provides tuition reimbursement using Remitly's platform.

## Navigating the 2021 IPO and Investor Relations
* **Don't Make the IPO the Goal:** Remitly went public in 2021 at a $7.8 billion valuation—just two weeks before the public markets "slammed shut" for several years. Oppenheimer kept IPO preparations tight, inviting ~75 team members and two or three of Remitly's earliest customers to the event to keep the focus on serving customers rather than market milestones.
* **Private-to-Public Cadence:** Even as a private company, Remitly treated angel and VC updates (initially monthly) as formal investor relations. That discipline, combined with listening to VCs who passed on earlier rounds—asking *why* and implementing their feedback—helped Remitly raise subsequent rounds and transition smoothly to quarterly public reporting.

## Transitioning From CEO to Chairman
* **Timing the Handoff:** After 15 years as CEO (including four years as a public company CEO), Oppenheimer transitioned to Chairman earlier this year (2026) while the business was performing strongly.
* **Chair, Not Executive Chair:** Oppenheimer intentionally avoided the "Executive Chair" title, calling it poorly defined and messy, and instead committed to being a true Chair who is "invited to the party" by the CEO rather than backseat driving.
* **Bringing in Sebastian:** To lead Remitly's expansion into broader financial services and AI-first reinvention (informed by Oppenheimer's involvement with the Seattle AI startup group *Foundations*), the board hired Sebastian, a mathematician who grew up in Argentina and brings deep operating experience:
  * Ran Oracle's Latin American business for 15 years, reporting to Larry Ellison.
  * Worked at Apple, reporting to Tim Cook and working closely with Steve Jobs.
  * Built Amazon's marketplace business over 10+ years, reporting directly to Jeff Bezos.
  * Served as Vice Chair and Co-CEO at WeWork.

## Filtering Advice and Mentoring Others
* **Handling Bad Advice:** Oppenheimer approaches feedback with a growth mindset, assuming everyone has a nugget of good advice even if they lack full context. When he hears bad advice, he pauses and asks "why" three to five times to uncover the underlying insight.
* **Paying It Forward:** To be a "Nittin" for someone else, Oppenheimer advises mentors to share their own lived experiences *before* giving advice so the recipient can connect the dots themselves.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **1–5 Year Product & Customer Expansion (Matt Oppenheimer):** Remitly will expand beyond core senders of a few hundred dollars into "growth accelerators," including:
  * Moving up-market (referencing HBS professor Clay Christensen's *The Innovator's Dilemma*) to serve high-value senders ($5,000 transactions), small businesses, and the 30 million receivers already on Remitly's network.
  * Expanding the product suite with the **Remitly card** (enabling stored value and multi-currency accounts over time) and **"send now, pay later"** products to help customers smooth cash flow.

## Notable Quotes
> "Companies are built by solving problems, and then you have to pivot on the solution. And I always knew I wanted to be an entrepreneur, but I wanted to find a problem that actually made a positive impact in the world. And my view is the road less traveled is how to find those problems." — Matt Oppenheimer

> "Going public has nothing to do with serving customers, and it also is at the whim of the markets. Markets open, markets closed. In fact, like two weeks after we went public, the market slammed shut for several years for companies our stage and size." — Matt Oppenheimer

> "You want to get invited to the party, not invite yourself to the party. And Sebastian is inviting me to incredible things that I can add value in, but he's the CEO." — Matt Oppenheimer

items.title: Minister Josephine Teo & Sierra CEO Clay Bavor at Silicon Valley & The World | Semafor
items.summary: Singapore is navigating new US chip restrictions and an ongoing export-control investigation while remaining a premier hub for AI companies like Sierra, as both policymakers and tech leaders grapple with data center sustainability, rapid workforce disruption, and building consumer trust in AI agents.
items.content_text:
**TL;DR**
Singapore is navigating new US chip restrictions and an ongoing export-control investigation while remaining a premier hub for AI companies like Sierra, as both policymakers and tech leaders grapple with data center sustainability, rapid workforce disruption, and building consumer trust in AI agents.

## US Chip Restrictions & The Mega Speed Investigation
*   **New US Export Controls:** Moderating the discussion, Associated Press Executive Editor Julie Pace noted the Trump administration's move earlier that day to restrict remote access to advanced US computing, chips, and servers, alongside new licensing requirements for chip sales in Singapore.
*   **Singapore’s Response:** Minister Josephine Teo stated Singapore is engaging affected businesses and US counterparts to clarify the rules and ensure "trusted access" to AI infrastructure for legitimate businesses.
    *   Teo emphasized Singapore's commitment to the rule of law, noting the country hosts roughly 6,000 US companies.
    *   Despite the new rules, Singapore's AI momentum remains strong, with OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind all announcing new activities there in the last couple of months.
*   **The Mega Speed Probe:** Teo detailed Singapore's independent investigation into Mega Speed, which began in February 2025.
    *   In June 2025, Singapore learned the US Bureau of Industry and Standards (BIS) was also interested in Mega Speed for post-shipment verification checks.
    *   Singapore requested US assistance regarding Mega Speed’s server movement declarations, specifically seeking cooperation from Super Micro, from whom they received "very little support and information."
    *   Teo met with US Deputy Secretary of State Kurt Campbell, and both agreed to keep lines of communication open as the investigation continues.

## Sierra’s Singapore Expansion & Enterprise Traction
*   **Why Singapore:** Sierra CEO Clay Bavor explained that his company chose Singapore for its Asia headquarters due to its business-friendly environment, investment incentives, ministry access, and major local enterprises—including DBS, Singapore Airlines, and Singtel (the latter two are Sierra customers).
    *   Sierra co-founder Bret Taylor was in Singapore at the time of the event launching the company's next phase.
*   **Enterprise Scale:** Bavor shared concrete metrics on Sierra's US footprint, noting the company serves 50% of the Fortune 50 and 40% of the Fortune 100.
    *   **Financial Services:** Sierra works with Rocket Mortgage to originate over $1 billion in new mortgages every month.
    *   **Healthcare:** Sierra partners with 4 out of the 5 largest US healthcare payers, using AI agents with "superhuman memory" to help patients navigate complex procedure eligibility.
*   **Agent Alignment:** Addressing Pace's question on whether AI agents serve the company or the consumer, Bavor argued the two are aligned: "You do right by customers, you do right by your business."
*   **Leadership & Nvidia:** When asked about his recent comments on singular leaders like Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and succession planning, Bavor deferred to Nvidia’s board of directors, calling it "above my paygrade."

## Data Center Pushback, Sustainability & Workforce Disruption
*   **A Destabilizing Force:** Responding to US mid-term election pushback against data centers and the pace of AI, Bavor acknowledged it is more than a communications issue. He noted that software engineers no longer write code—now called "hand coding"—a shift that seemed wild just 18 months ago.
*   **Regional Data Center Pushback:** Teo noted that objections to data centers are also occurring in neighboring Thailand and Malaysia, outlining Singapore’s three-part strategy:
    *   Recognize that unlimited data center growth is incompatible with climate commitments.
    *   Focus on greener data centers by using less energy or greener energy.
    *   Invest serious R&D funding into "resource-efficient AI" to optimize operations and how computing is performed.
*   **Workforce Strategy:** Teo advocated for looking at the workforce in totality—attracting new growth industries like Sierra while fostering a culture of "shared responsibility" among individuals, companies showing solidarity with employees, and government resource support.

## Personal AI Habits & Boundaries
*   **Minister Josephine Teo:** Uses a news agent that scans roughly 16,000 articles a day (while compensating for its "narrow aperture"). However, she is not comfortable letting her email-connected agent make payments yet, preferring to "hold on to my purse for now."
*   **Clay Bavor:** Regularly uses the prompt *"help me deeply appreciate X"* before watching a movie, listening to music, or eating a meal, claiming it makes him enjoy things 30% more. He is not yet comfortable having an AI agent read his email.

## Notable Quotes
> "It is not just communicating better about something, it is a destabilizing force and it's happening quickly." — Clay Bavor, CEO of Sierra

> "You cannot have unlimited growth in data centers, particularly for a country like Singapore that is very serious about its climate commitments." — Minister Josephine Teo

> "I have an agent that also is connected to my email. And it will very often be so enthusiastic drafting emails for me to respond to... even volunteering to make payments for me. I'm not comfortable with that yet. I'm going to hold on to my purse for now." — Minister Josephine Teo

items.title: Mistral CEO Arthur Mensch at Silicon Valley & The World | Semafor
items.summary: Mistral CEO Arthur Mensch outlines the company's differentiation as a "sovereign AI" provider—offering portable, zero-trust, on-premise, and open-weight models for critical industrial and financial workflows—while positioning Europe as a vital hedge against US and Chinese AI dependencies ahead of an eventual European IPO.
items.content_text:
**TL;DR**
Mistral CEO Arthur Mensch outlines the company's differentiation as a "sovereign AI" provider—offering portable, zero-trust, on-premise, and open-weight models for critical industrial and financial workflows—while positioning Europe as a vital hedge against US and Chinese AI dependencies ahead of an eventual European IPO.

---

## US Presence & Enterprise Strategy: "Sovereign AI"
* **Silicon Valley Footprint:** Mistral maintains its US headquarters in Palo Alto with a sizable team of researchers and go-to-market staff.
  * The company is increasingly partnering with cyber vendors to deploy its latest open-source release, which Mensch noted has strong cyber capabilities.
* **Defining "Sovereign AI":** Rather than competing on sheer scale with OpenAI/Anthropic or strictly on price with Chinese labs, Mistral targets mission-critical enterprise processes (such as R&D and manufacturing) with three guarantees: portability, business continuity, and affordability.
  * **Industrial Customers:** Mistral powers agentic engineering loops and physical simulations for major manufacturers, including **Airbus** (aircraft), **ASML** (lithography machines), and **BMW** (automobiles).
* **Horizontal vs. Vertical Model:** Mensch contrasted Mistral's horizontal, open-weight platform—which lets customers build custom systems—against competitors that go vertical to capture more of the value chain.

## Data Privacy, Portability & Competitive Positioning
* **Zero-Trust Architecture:** Addressing Shelly Banjo's question on whether OpenAI and Anthropic use customer data to build competing products, Mensch noted that enterprise clients in manufacturing and financial services do not want to rely on vendor promises.
  * Mistral proves it cannot see customer data either by deploying models **on-premises** (so data never flows back to Mistral) or through **confidential cloud guarantees**.
  * This ensures customers' IP and processes continue running even if Mistral were to disappear, and protects them if a vendor suffers a cyberattack.
* **Two-Tier Model Portfolio:** While Mistral's core platform is portable by design, it operates two distinct model categories:
  * **Open-source models:** Available for free.
  * **Proprietary models:** Specialized models deployed on-premises for customers rather than exposed for free.
* **Pricing:** Mensch emphasized that Mistral's models—as well as the third-party open-source models it serves—are "quite cheap."

## Geopolitics & Hedging Against US/China Dependencies
* **Global vs. Regional Drivers:** While Mistral's US growth is driven purely by technological differentiation, its growth in Europe and Asia is also fueled by geopolitical fragmentation.
* **Hedging Supply Chain Risk:** European and Asian enterprises are actively hedging against excessive reliance on US providers, fearing they could lose access to US models or compute.
  * Customers increasingly demand compute located in Europe and operated by European players.

## French Politics, Youth Employment & European IPO Plans
* **Youth & AI Anxiety:** Responding to Banjo's question on political unrest in France, Mensch attributed part of the youth anguish to companies freezing entry-level hiring in favor of senior staff due to AI, alongside unsustainable European pension systems.
  * Mistral actively hires young talent, arguing they adopt AI far better and create "much more value than people that are 10 years older than them."
  * Mensch criticized "Doomsday" AI narratives for fueling public anxiety.
* **Navigating French Politics:** Pushing back on the idea that Mistral is a "personal project" of President Emmanuel Macron, Mensch said sovereign AI is a bipartisan necessity to avoid trade imbalances and foreign dependency.
  * Ahead of France's **2027** presidential election, Mensch has been conducting **1-hour** education sessions with political candidates to prepare them for "five years of very technical discussions" on AI policy and data center capacity.
* **European IPO:** Europe represents Mistral's headquarters, the majority of its investor base, and "a little more than half" of its customer base, making it the natural listing venue.

---

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **European IPO Timeline:** Mistral is preparing to go public in Europe, though it will not happen this year — *Arthur Mensch* ("We're not going to do this this year, but we're definitely getting ready for it.")
* **AI Policymaking Horizon:** The next French administration will face five years of highly technical AI policy discussions — *Arthur Mensch* ("They need to get a little more technical because that's going to be five years of very technical discussions.")

---

## Notable Quotes
> "They don't need to trust us because we have basically a zero-trust agreement with them." — *Arthur Mensch*

> "I think it's actually pretty bad decisions for companies to stop hiring young people... because you can invest on them, they will use AI much better and they will create a lot of value, much more value than people that are 10 years older than them." — *Arthur Mensch*

> "You can't afford to only import that technology. It creates too much trade imbalance and it creates too much dependency." — *Arthur Mensch*

items.title: OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar at Silicon Valley & The World | Semafor
items.summary: OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar detailed the company's path to profitability and an eventual IPO, highlighting $122 billion in Q1 fundraising, a $1.25 trillion valuation in its latest opportunistic round, 1.2 billion weekly ChatGPT users, and a $1 billion advertising run rate achieved in under 200 days.
items.content_text:
**TL;DR:** OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar detailed the company's path to profitability and an eventual IPO, highlighting $122 billion in Q1 fundraising, a $1.25 trillion valuation in its latest opportunistic round, 1.2 billion weekly ChatGPT users, and a $1 billion advertising run rate achieved in under 200 days. To offset massive compute expenses, OpenAI is driving high-margin enterprise and ad revenue while building its own custom chip, Halapeno, to lower supply costs.

## Fundraising, Valuation, and IPO Strategy
* **Capitalization & Valuation:** OpenAI raised $122 billion in Q1 and is closing out an opportunistic fundraising round at a $1.25 trillion valuation.
  * Friar noted the latest round was unplanned and triggered by an inaccurate news story that generated investor inbounds, prompting OpenAI to execute a rapid, six-week raise ahead of the midterms.
* **Anthropic IPO & Market Access:** Responding to Semafor Executive Editor Gina Chon on Anthropic's upcoming IPO, Friar wished them well, calling it positive for the ecosystem because public market investors currently lack direct access to frontier model companies (having to invest in chips, infrastructure, or hyperscalers instead).
* **OpenAI IPO Criteria:** Friar views an IPO as a milestone toward OpenAI's mission of AGI for the benefit of humanity, which will also unlock debt-based financing and lower the overall cost of capital. She outlined four readiness criteria:
  * Business readiness (which she believes OpenAI has achieved).
  * Momentum (demonstrated by Q3 performance).
  * Market readiness.
  * Safety and alignment, noting that remaining private allows OpenAI to pace itself on safety work while staying well-capitalized.

## Consumer Scale, Advertising, and Search Growth
* **User & Subscriber Base:** ChatGPT reaches 1.2 billion weekly users, adding 200 million users in Q3 alone, with over 100 million paying subscribers.
  * 90% of ChatGPT's customers are outside the U.S.
  * Weekly usage includes 300 million people asking health or wellness questions and 200 million asking personal finance questions, with interaction modes increasingly shifting toward voice.
* **Advertising Business:** With 90% of its user base on free tiers, OpenAI launched an advertising model that hit a $1 billion run rate in August—reaching that milestone in under 200 days, making it OpenAI's fastest-growing business.
  * Ads are now live in 87 countries, delivering high contextual and personal relevance.
* **Search Momentum:** ChatGPT now handles roughly 20% of the volume of all Google queries, up from approximately 11% in March.

## Enterprise Momentum and Product Roadmap
* **Enterprise Growth:** OpenAI's enterprise business grew 100% quarter-over-quarter in Q3 and is already a highly profitable model, supported by frontier APIs and a growing system integrator ecosystem (e.g., Capgemini).
* **Cybersecurity & Astros:** Cyber is a top priority for boards and C-suites. OpenAI released its most capable cyber model, **Astros** (branded as **Daybreak, Red and Blue**), which scores 100% on cyber benchmarks.
  * In Q3, OpenAI signed cyber-led deals with JP Morgan Chase and Visa, and expanded work with existing customer Amgen.
  * In August, OpenAI discovered two PHP vulnerabilities that, if left unpatched, could have taken down roughly 70% of the internet.
* **Agentic Coding & Virtual Coworkers ("Dots"):** 
  * Friar emphasized that coding has shifted to autonomous, agentic workflows, predicting that manual coding will soon feel like hand-knitting compared to using a machine.
  * OpenAI is rolling out **dots**—proactive virtual coworkers that sweep Slack and Gmail to prepare talking points and track tasks. After using dots for 6–8 weeks, Friar compared their necessity to Excel or email.
* **Vertical Expansion:** OpenAI is expanding into verticals including life sciences, manufacturing, the Office of the CLO, and the Office of the CFO.

## Compute Economics and Custom Silicon
* **Demand vs. Supply:** Addressing Chon's question on whether revenue can catch up to astronomical compute expenses, Friar stated that OpenAI has been short on compute in 2026 and must invest ahead of demand.
* **Custom Chip (Halapeno):** OpenAI is building its own chip, **Halapeno**, to enable "soup-to-nuts" self-builds.
  * This shrinks the timeline from demand signal to supply signal, eliminates third-party margin stacking, and strengthens OpenAI's negotiating leverage with hyperscalers.

## Public Trust, Foundation, and Community Engagement
* **OpenAI Foundation:** Created during last year's recapitalization, the OpenAI Foundation holds roughly $180 billion in value and is actively issuing grants in life sciences and the public good.
* **Georgia Data Center & Local Impact:** Responding to Chon on public distrust of AI, Friar stressed the need to show up in communities—citing OpenAI's potential ~3 gigawatt data center in Georgia.
  * **Water & Power:** A 1-gigawatt data center uses about two Olympic swimming pools' worth of water, which OpenAI will truck in and recirculate like a car radiator (with most water going to workers). OpenAI also pledged not to raise local electricity bills and is working with grid providers to potentially lower costs.
  * **Community Investment:** In Effingham County, Georgia, OpenAI sponsored free school lunches and breakfasts for all public school students (driving a 70% uptick in participation), sponsored a local park, and hosted an AI summit for small businesses.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **AGI Multimodality:** "AGI will be multimodal. It will be LLMs, but it will be voice, it will be image." — Sarah Friar
* **Gross Margin Expansion:** Advertising will have "a really strong kind of upward push on gross margins overall" next year by covering the costs of free users. — Sarah Friar
* **Voice-Driven Interaction:** The mode of how consumers ask questions is turning to voice, which Friar identified as a key direction for the technology "over the next year or two." — Sarah Friar

## Notable Quotes
> "Research I always say it's a breakthrough business, not a roadmap business." — Sarah Friar

> "If you want to code with your hands, that sounds lovely. Do it because you like it, but if you're going to code in my company, you better be coding autonomously, like, even ideally just using voice as your coding language of choice." — Sarah Friar

> "When you go talk to people in real life, and show up for them, you have a very different conversation, and I believe a very different outcome." — Sarah Friar

items.title: OpenAI’s Cofounder & Research Chief Explain Self-Improving AI
items.summary: Frontier AI labs have entered a "Centaur era" where AI acts as "research interns" roughly 25–50% of the way toward full recursive self-improvement (RSI).
items.content_text:
## TL;DR
Frontier AI labs have entered a "Centaur era" where AI acts as "research interns" roughly 25–50% of the way toward full recursive self-improvement (RSI). While AI is already accelerating research—delivering an estimated 2x speedup—achieving full RSI requires overcoming bottlenecks in "research taste," downstream evaluation, and compute, even as automated research emerges as one of the most promising tools for solving AI alignment.

## Defining RSI and the "Centaur Era"
* **The Current State of Acceleration:** According to a November 5 Metr report cited by a16z general partner Sarah Wang, AI research at Anthropic has seen a roughly 2x speedup in the rate of progress over the past year, driven by human researchers using AI models to accelerate their workflows.
* **RSI as an Accelerator:** Mark Chen, Chief Research Officer at OpenAI (who has been with the company for over eight years and co-leading research with Jakub Pachocki since 2025), defines RSI primarily as using AI—such as Codex—to accelerate pre-training and reinforcement learning (RL) and shift the capability curve.
* **"AI Research Interns":** Chen notes that OpenAI has built "AI research interns" today, measured by the amount of compute managed end-to-end by Codex to run scoped experiments, monitor runs, and automate parts of the research pipeline.
* **The AGI vs. RSI Spectrum:** Chen views both AGI and RSI as spectrums rather than single moments in time. While he estimates the industry is roughly 80% of the way to AGI, he places current capabilities at only 25–50% along the RSI spectrum.
* **The Centaur Workflow:** John Schulman, co-founder and Chief Scientist of Thinking Machines Lab and co-founder of OpenAI, describes the current phase as the "Centaur era," where an expert human working with AI outperforms either alone.
  * *Concrete Example:* Schulman shared his workflow using Fable (with settings like UltraCode turned up) to run experiments for several days. While the AI generates reasonable experiments and ideas, the end result often fails until Schulman steps in to read the results, ask questions the AI missed, and redirect the project.

## Bottlenecks to Full RSI: Taste, Verification, and Compute
* **The "Research Taste" Gap:** Schulman defines research taste as knowing which ideas are important long-term, generalizable, and composable with other ideas—as opposed to routine execution or hyperparameter optimization.
  * *Knowledge vs. Experience:* While AI can read and memorize all historical literature, it lacks the human experience of making predictions, being wrong, and absorbing those lessons.
  * *Baking in Intuition:* To bridge this gap, Schulman expects companies will use RL from human feedback (RLHF) to collect data from researchers on which proposed ideas are good, effectively baking human intuition into models.
* **Verification and Evaluation:** Chen identifies measuring success as one of the defining challenges of RSI.
  * *Pre-training vs. Downstream:* Pre-training is straightforward to hill-climb because the field relies on a single metric: perplexity. Downstream, however, evaluation benchmarks have increasingly shorter shelf-lives, forcing labs to focus heavily on automating the creation of new, harder evals.
* **Compute Constraints:** Unlike math—where hypotheses can be tested purely through reasoning—AI research resembles experimental physics or biology, requiring physical experiments. Chen notes that accelerating RSI requires finding smaller-scale experiments that reliably predict larger-scale outcomes.

## Aligning RSI—and Using AI to Solve Alignment
* **The Risks of Drift:** Chen warns that without solving goal and value alignment, models running over long horizons could drift and develop dangerous sub-objectives, such as attempting to exfiltrate themselves or copy weights outside of OpenAI.
* **Stronger Models Aligning Models:** Chen argues that RSI must be deeply embedded in the alignment loop, noting that chain-of-thought monitorability is currently the most effective alignment tool. He is also encouraged by an organic shift of researchers from pre-training and RL into safety and alignment sub-teams.
* **Optimizing for Honesty:** Schulman is optimistic about designing training objectives that incentivize models to report on their internal states. He highlights OpenAI's *Confessions* research—where models are rewarded solely for the honesty of a self-reported confession without penalizing the main answer's reward—alongside techniques like natural language autoencoders and counterfactual simulability.
* **Automated Alignment Breakthroughs:** Wang highlights August research from Anthropic showing that automated AI researchers discovered fixes for 10 different alignment failures. Some of these fixes transferred to models nearly 5x larger, and the best automated methods outperformed experienced human researchers.
* **Decentralized Alignment:** Schulman's Thinking Machines Lab is building customizable models based on the view that people hold different values and should have control over their AI's values. He advocates for making alignment a "public science" so the industry does not overfit to the conclusions of a few companies.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **2027 Capability Inflection:** A chart cited by Sarah Wang projects that in 2027, OpenAI's frontier model capabilities will begin a steep climb set off by automated AI research.
* **Compute Bottlenecks and Next-Gen Inflection:** Mark Chen predicts that AI capabilities will continue to rise until they become bounded by compute, followed by another major inflection point when AIs begin accelerating compute itself (such as helping build next-generation data centers).
* **RLHF for Research Taste:** John Schulman predicts companies will use RL from human feedback to collect data from human researchers on idea quality to instill research intuition into models.
* **Enduring Role of Human Judgment:** Sarah Wang concludes that human judgment will remain essential for the foreseeable future, despite rapid capability acceleration.

## Notable Quotes
> "We're very much in this Centaur era where AI has phenomenal capabilities, it's superhuman in a lot of ways, but when you have an expert human working with the AI, you get even better results." — John Schulman

> "I do believe that we've built AI research interns today... When you ask me, I feel like we're maybe 80% of the way when I think about this AGI spectrum. I think we're earlier in the RSI spectrum... maybe we're somewhere between, let's say, 25 and 50% there." — Mark Chen

> "When we look at what's the most effective tool for aligning models, it is chain-of-thought monitorability today. So, when we think about the future of alignment, it has to be stronger models aligning other models. It does kind of feel like RSI must be intricately and deeply in this loop in some way." — Mark Chen

> "I do think that RSI could be the key to solving alignment... I think human judgment will still matter a lot for the foreseeable future." — Sarah Wang

items.title: Palmer Luckey: How Steve Jobs Ruined Everything, the $2B Oculus Sale & Getting Fired From Facebook
items.summary: In a wide-ranging conversation with Walter Isaacson, Anduril founder Palmer Luckey explains how getting fired from Facebook led him to build a product-first defense tech giant, why he believes autonomous weapons make warfare more humane, and why Steve Jobs’ iPhone design set human-computer interaction on a backwards course.
items.content_text:
**TL;DR:** In a wide-ranging conversation with Walter Isaacson, Anduril founder Palmer Luckey explains how getting fired from Facebook led him to build a product-first defense tech giant, why he believes autonomous weapons make warfare more humane, and why Steve Jobs’ iPhone design set human-computer interaction on a backwards course.

## Early Roots, Homeschooling & The $2B Oculus Sale
* **Homeschooling & Mod Retro:** Luckey credits homeschooling for allowing him to take high school and college credits simultaneously at ages 14–15, freeing up time to build VR prototypes in a camper trailer.
  * He recruited Oculus’s early hardware engineers—including first employee Chris Dicus—from *Mod Retro*, an online electronics forum he founded.
  * He was heavily influenced by tech-centric sci-fi like Jules Verne’s *20,000 Leagues Under the Sea* and *Star Trek*, noting he was born at the exact right moment to turn VR from sci-fi into reality.
* **Why Facebook Over Google or Microsoft:** When Luckey sold Oculus for roughly $2 billion in 2014 at age 21, he chose Facebook because it lacked its own OS or hardware platform and *needed* VR to succeed.
  * Facebook guaranteed $1 billion per year in R&D for 10 years ($10 billion total), but ultimately spent roughly $70 billion over the decade.
  * By contrast, Google shut down its VR program ~1.5 years after the Oculus acquisition, restarted it, and killed it again.
* **Meta’s Reality Labs Layoffs:** Luckey defended Meta’s recent 10% layoff at Reality Labs, noting the remaining 90% is still 10x larger than the next biggest VR competitor.
  * While calling *Meta Horizons* a "terrible product," he argued that cutting first-party gaming apps is healthy for the ecosystem, as Meta will no longer compete directly with third-party developers like Ubisoft, Rockstar, and Capcom.
* **Getting Fired & Side Hustles:** Fired from Facebook at 24 after donating $9,000–$10,000 to a Trump-supporting PAC, Luckey chose not to sue and spend five years as a "professional full-time victim," opting instead to start Anduril.
  * Anduril takes up 99% of his time, with 1% spent on side projects: manufacturing a high-end Nintendo Gameboy tribute via *Mod Retro* (featuring a sapphire screen lens and magnesium aluminum alloy shell) and co-owning a niche ice cream burrito company.

## How Steve Jobs "Ruined Everything"
* **The Low Skill Ceiling:** Responding to Walter Isaacson’s theory that human-computer interfaces drive technological progress, Luckey argued the industry has gone in the wrong direction since the iPhone.
  * The iPhone optimized for a 1-minute learning curve and 10-minute mastery, eliminating incentives for users to spend 1,000 to 50,000 hours mastering a tool for superhuman output.
  * Luckey admitted his own Oculus Rift followed this same low-barrier-to-entry model and argued that brain-computer interfaces like Neuralink are making the same mistake.

## Anduril, Autonomous Weapons & Deterrence
* **A Product-First Defense Model:** Luckey founded Anduril with Trae Stephens of Founders Fund (who had previously met with ~2,000 defense startups and made zero investments).
  * Unlike traditional contractors, Anduril operates like SpaceX or Palantir—investing billions of its own capital upfront (e.g., developing aircraft for 5 years before receiving a dime from the government).
  * Anduril’s AI-powered fighter jet, *Fury* (Air Force designation *FQ-44*), recently beat Northrop Grumman, Boeing, and Lockheed Martin for the U.S. Air Force’s Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) Increment One contract.
* **The Lattice Platform:** *Lattice* is the AI software brain powering Anduril’s 25+ hardware products (missiles, submarines, fighter jets, sensor towers), allowing every sensor to act as an eye for every other system.
  * Anduril employs as many people on Lattice as it does on all of its hardware products combined.
* **The Morality of Autonomous Weapons:** Luckey argued that autonomous weapons are the only rational moral choice because they reduce collateral damage and civilian deaths compared to "dumb" weapons.
  * Challenging U.S. military doctrine’s "human-in-the-loop" requirement (such as remotely piloted Predator drones), he noted that radio links create cyber vulnerabilities and that the U.S. has used autonomous radiation-seeking missiles since Vietnam.
  * He equated AI targeting to thousands-of-years-old autonomous traps (like pit traps designed to let foot soldiers pass while collapsing under horses/officers) and landmines, stressing that humans must still be held accountable for how force is deployed.
* **Deterrence Over Credit:** Luckey believes modern precision warfare has already reduced casualties by ~90% compared to World War II. Anduril’s ultimate goal is deterrence—meaning if the U.S. avoids a war with China over the next 20 years, Anduril succeeded, even if it receives little credit.

## AI’s Greatest Risk & Future Bets
* **Bioweapons & AI:** While generally anti-censorship, Luckey identified AI-enabled biological and chemical weapons as his #1 fear.
  * AI can already guide lab technicians ("meat robots") through pharmacological experiments without requiring PhDs, raising the risk of bad actors designing targeted bioweapons.
  * He advocated tampering with or restricting dangerous biological data outside approved institutions to prevent this.
* **Vertical Integration & Seasteading:** Asked by Isaacson to pick the next big breakthroughs, Luckey highlighted two areas:
  * **Ultra-cheap manufacturing:** Vertically integrating power generation, manufacturing, processing, and recycling to mirror the textile industry (which made fabric ~1,000x cheaper).
  * **Settling the oceans:** Using new material science to build maintenance-free mega-structures at sea that last for thousands of years.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **Anduril Contract Wins:** "You're going to see us winning major programs I think on a regular cadence because investments that we've made over the last eight years are finally bearing out." — Palmer Luckey
* **The Future of War Casualties:** "We're going to get to a point where most of the casualties are going to be robots and systems and hardware rather than flesh and bone." — Palmer Luckey
* **$1,000 Cars:** "I think a world where you can buy a car for a thousand dollars is something that... is actually within our lifetime." — Palmer Luckey
* **Seasteading Comeback:** "We're going to get to the point where we're able to build mega structures at sea that persist for thousands of years without any significant maintenance... seasteading... will come back." — Palmer Luckey

## Notable Quotes
> "I had to make a choice: was I going to be a professional victim, or was I going to start a new company and prove that I'm not a one-hit wonder, that I'm not the dummy that people said that I was." — Palmer Luckey

> "Steve Jobs ruined everything with the iPhone. We're still suffering the impacts of his incredible product design." — Palmer Luckey

> "By the time you're fighting a war, it means you didn't build your garden correctly." — Palmer Luckey

items.title: Perplexity CEO and Founder Aravind Srinivas at Silicon Valley & The World | Semafor
items.summary: Perplexity CEO Aravind Srinivas revealed that the company just crossed $1 billion in annual run rate (ARR) with 5x lower burn than its major IPO-bound competitor, driven by a capital-efficient, model-neutral "agent orchestration" strategy.
items.content_text:
## TL;DR
Perplexity CEO Aravind Srinivas revealed that the company just crossed $1 billion in annual run rate (ARR) with 5x lower burn than its major IPO-bound competitor, driven by a capital-efficient, model-neutral "agent orchestration" strategy. To maintain this momentum, Perplexity is committing at least 10,000 GPUs to a new frontier research program while expanding into air-gapped, on-premises local AI for regulated enterprises.

## Financial Milestones & Capital Efficiency
* **Crossing $1 Billion ARR:** Srinivas announced on stage that Perplexity crossed $1 billion in annual run rate on the day of the interview, noting their cash burn to reach that milestone was 5x lower than "the company that's going to IPO this week."
* **Gross Margin Expansion:**
  * **Paid Users:** Currently at 56% gross margins on the $1 billion ARR.
  * **Blended (Including Free Users):** Flipped from -219% in Q4 2025 to 17% in Q3 2026, with expectations to climb further as Perplexity trains more of its own models.
* **In-House Infrastructure Savings:** Perplexity built its own model, compute clusters, post-training models, and inference stack for quick, fast search—currently serving 80% to 90% of its traffic and saving at least $100 million to $200 million annually.
* **Lean Headcount:** The company operates with roughly 500 employees, which Srinivas described as a "sweet spot" that provides researchers ample compute per person without requiring trillion-dollar CAPEX commitments.

## Agent Orchestration & The Frontier Research Program
* **The "Mode-Neutral" Moat:** In response to moderator Ben Smith's question about competing against hyperscalers in the agent space, Srinivas argued that Perplexity's moat is accuracy and model-neutral orchestration. Unlike hyperscalers—who are incentivized to lock users into their own clouds or equity-backed models to recoup massive CAPEX—Perplexity is strictly user-aligned.
* **10,000 GPU Commitment:** Perplexity announced a new frontier research program committing at least 10,000 GPUs to post-train models specifically for multi-agent orchestration and continual learning.
* **Open-Weight vs. Frontier Models:** 
  * Srinivas noted Perplexity's thinking on Chinese open-weight models has evolved beyond its earlier "1776" uncensored DeepSeek R1 project, shifting focus to agent sandbox security, accuracy, and reducing tool-call error rates.
  * **Benchmarking GLM vs. Opus:** Currently, post-trained GLM models (GLM 53 / GLM 31) take about 15 minutes to complete a task that Opus 55 finishes in 3 minutes, largely because GLM wastes time on erroneous tool calls.

## Local AI, On-Prem Agents & The Compute Debate
* **Air-Gapped Enterprise Security:** Perplexity is partnering with companies like NVIDIA to deploy fully local, air-gapped, on-premises agents for regulated institutions—including sovereign wealth funds, banks, credit card companies, exchanges, insurance firms, and pharma/bio companies—that cannot risk sending proprietary data or IP to frontier labs for post-training.
* **Escalation & Hybrid Frameworks:**
  * **Local-to-Cloud Escalation:** Local models can request user permission to orchestrate up to cloud frontier models when a task requires higher intelligence.
  * **Hybrid Mode:** Released on Apple Silicon, allowing users to default to frontier cloud models and orchestrate down to local hardware for sensitive data.
* **Jevons Paradox & AI Compute:** Addressing Smith's question on whether the industry is overbuilding compute, Srinivas argued that local AI will not pop the AI bubble. Instead, Jevons Paradox will take effect: lowering the cost of AI will drive massive adoption among small businesses and expand overall usage of frontier AI as a gateway.

## Media Relations & Ecosystem Integration
* **Pre-Training vs. Summarization:** Pressed by Ben Smith on media lawsuits and Perplexity's 2025 revenue-share program, Srinivas emphasized that Perplexity does not pre-train on or distill books and publisher content. Instead, it provides answers and summaries with citations, arguing that while answer engines naturally have lower click-through rates than link-based search, they create a positive flywheel of curiosity and reading.
* **Premium Connectors:** Perplexity is expanding its role as an orchestrator across all data sources—including the web, CRMs, Slack, and premium connectors like the *New England Journal of Medicine*.

## Leadership Lessons
* **Jensen Huang's Grit:** Reflecting on NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang's advice, Srinivas praised Huang's relentlessness and "day-one" paranoia—operating even the world's most valuable company as if it could go out of business in 30 days—calling him one of the greatest founders in American history.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **Open-Weight Parity:** "Expect there to be an open weight model as good as Opus 55 in 6 to 12 months... 6 to 8 months is a good estimate. But by the time, there will be Opus 6, there will be Opus 65." — Aravind Srinivas
* **On-Prem Hardware:** "We're going to see systems that can run in few megawatts of power and draw a lot of like, you know, capabilities and keep your data isolated." — Aravind Srinivas
* **Next Frontier Domains:** "Frontier labs are going to push the boundaries in new domains outside of coding and knowledge work like biology, chips, robots, and a lot more value is going to get unlocked there." — Aravind Srinivas
* **Local AI Driving Frontier Growth:** "As more and more people start using local AI, it's probably going to lead to an expansion in the user of frontier AI as well." — Aravind Srinivas

## Notable Quotes
> "We just crossed a billion dollars in annual run rate today... Our burn to get to a billion dollars in annual run rate is 5x lower [than the company that's going to IPO this week]." — Aravind Srinivas

> "We're the only mode neutral, accurate agent orchestrator out there." — Aravind Srinivas

> "You can only provably have full control if you have it inside your own premises... It's just like your refrigerator at home." — Aravind Srinivas

> "Our product actually doesn't replace journalism, it only like expands it." — Aravind Srinivas

items.title: Why Airtable’s founder is betting on teams of AI agents
items.summary: Airtable founder Howie Liu sold his nearly $500M-revenue SaaS company to Bending Spoons because the AI era has fundamentally rewritten software economics, distribution, and pricing models.
items.content_text:
**TL;DR**
Airtable founder Howie Liu sold his nearly $500M-revenue SaaS company to Bending Spoons because the AI era has fundamentally rewritten software economics, distribution, and pricing models. He has now spun out Hyperagent to bet on "multiplayer" AI—teams of autonomous, role-specific agents designed to augment small business owner-operators rather than compete in the crowded personal assistant market.

## Selling Airtable to Bending Spoons
* **End of the SaaS Golden Era:** Liu founded Airtable in 2012 at the dawn of product-led growth (PLG) and rich browser-based single-page apps (alongside Figma and Miro). While Airtable reached nearly $500M in revenue, generated strong cash flow, and was still growing, Liu saw it as a mature business built on SaaS-era assumptions (like seat-based pricing) that are being disrupted by AI.
* **Why Bending Spoons:** Liu chose Bending Spoons—a publicly traded US company known for buying and holding brands forever (including Evernote, Vimeo, WeTransfer, AOL, and Miro)—because they are transparent, high-integrity, and disciplined about their playbook, avoiding the antitrust risks or drawn-out diligence traps seen in deals like Figma/Adobe.
* **Valuation & Equity Mechanics:** Airtable sold below its peak ZIRP-era valuation, a reality Liu believes many SaaS companies will face. However, because Airtable had raised over $1B and kept the vast majority of that cash on its balance sheet, the company was able to clear its preference stack and return dollars to common shareholders.
* **Spin-Out Structure:** Rather than keeping Hyperagent inside Airtable, Liu spun it out and gave Airtable shareholders a piece of upside in the new AI-native company.

## The Economics of SaaS vs. AI-Native Startups
* **Capital as a Crutch:** Liu argued against using Airtable’s cash flow to fund Hyperagent internally, noting that capital is rarely the primary constraint for 0-to-1 product-market fit and can actually distract from obsessive product iteration.
* **Structural Differences:** Traditional SaaS enjoys high margins and near-zero marginal distribution costs. AI-native businesses have fundamentally different margin profiles (due to variable token/compute spend), pricing models (outcome/autonomy-based vs. seat-based), and go-to-market motions.
* **Seed-Stage Discipline:** Hyperagent raised a small round ("many tens of millions of dollars") mostly from insiders after spinning out, operating with a lean, seed-stage mentality rather than relying on incumbent scale.

## Hyperagent 2.0: Betting on Multiplayer Agents
* **Origin Story:** Hyperagent began during the winter holidays when Liu used frontier models (like Claude Code, Cursor, and Opus 4.5) to build real, structurally sound software solo—an "inside-out" approach driven by new technological capabilities rather than traditional MBA-style "outside-in" product planning.
* **Escaping the "Knife Fight in a Phone Booth":** Liu is intentionally avoiding the 1-to-1 personal AI assistant market (e.g., ChatGPT Dots at $100/month, Instinct in private beta, Claw Duet, Muse), where tech giants like Meta, Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Microsoft are subsidizing compute with tens of billions of dollars.
* **From 1.0 to 2.0:** While Hyperagent 1.0 was praised for deep customizability, Liu acknowledged it was overly complex and intimidating. The upcoming Hyperagent 2.0 is a near-total rebuild focused on **multiplayer agents** with smart defaults:
  * **Distinct Identities:** Each agent acts like a hired employee with its own identity, provisioned accounts, guardrails, and auditability.
  * **Multi-Agent Coordination:** Business owners can hold group chats or group calls with multiple agents at once, allowing a marketing agent and a sales agent to coordinate work.
* **Dogfooding at Hyperagent:** Liu uses Hyperagent agents 24/7 for strategy, generating Super Bowl-quality video ads, tracking competitors, and even writing merge-ready pull requests directly into Hyperagent's codebase.

## Target Market: Empowering SMB Owner-Operators
* **Deprioritizing Enterprise:** Unlike Airtable, which scaled into Fortune 500 enterprises, Hyperagent is targeting SMB owner-operators (e.g., landscapers, insurance brokers, designers, creative agencies) to enable rapid product iteration and self-serve adoption.
* **Augmenting, Not Replacing:** Small business owners don't want another CRM; they want another hire they can't otherwise afford. Early users report getting the output of 10 incremental hires.
* **Concrete Use Case (Landscaping):** An agent can take a client inquiry, pull satellite imagery and past Zillow photos, use image models to mock up a landscaping design, estimate pricing, and send a polished proposal immediately—undercutting competitors who take five weeks just to call back—while also managing ongoing field project schedules.

## Predictions & Forward Calls
* **AI's Economic Multiplier:** AI will double, triple, or potentially 10x the tens of trillions of dollars of human intelligence contribution to global GDP each year. — *Howie Liu*
* **Competitive Advantage:** Businesses in any category—even lower-margin ones like landscaping or insurance—that figure out how to deploy agents effectively will gain a 2x up to a 10x–100x advantage in efficiency, speed, and growth over competitors. — *Howie Liu*
* **SaaS Valuation Risk:** Many independent SaaS companies valued highly during the ZIRP era will never reach those peak valuations again, and attempting to maintain the status quo in the AI era risks underperforming the S&P 500 or eroding equity value. — *Howie Liu*

## Notable Quotes
> "I think single player is a knife fight in a phone booth... personally, I don't want to compete against Zuck and Alex and Nat Friedman over there... they have a boatload of money." — *Howie Liu*

> "I think AI is coming for everyone and everything... to not sell, even though that's kind of the default from inaction, is a different and also possibly riskier bet." — *Howie Liu*

> "Every business that figures this out, and they could be in any industry, any category, is going to have like not just a 2X but like quite literally an increasing up to like 10 to 100X advantage against their competition." — *Howie Liu*

items.title: World Labs Co-Founder & CEO Fei-Fei Li at Silicon Valley & The World | Semafor
items.summary: Following the close of AMD's $8.2 billion acquisition of World Labs, newly appointed AMD Chief Scientist Fei-Fei Li outlines how spatial intelligence and "world models" represent the next frontier of AI beyond language, while warning that universities are being priced out of AI research and calling for science-based governance.
items.content_text:
**TL;DR**
Following the close of AMD's $8.2 billion acquisition of World Labs, newly appointed AMD Chief Scientist Fei-Fei Li outlines how spatial intelligence and "world models" represent the next frontier of AI beyond language, while warning that universities are being priced out of AI research and calling for science-based governance.

## The $8.2B AMD Acquisition & Chip Ecosystem
* **Deal & New Role:** World Labs, which Li spent two and a half years building, announced an $8.2 billion deal to sell to AMD in September; the deal closed on Friday, making this interview day two of Li's tenure as Chief Scientist at AMD.
* **Strategic Rationale:** Li and AMD CEO Lisa Su view the partnership as "1+1 bigger than 3," extending far beyond simple access to compute.
  * **Co-Design:** The focus is on platform, infrastructure, and the co-evolution between AI models, software, and hardware, alongside expanding AMD's open ecosystem.
* **Multi-Chip Ecosystem:** Asked by moderator Andrew Edgecliffe-Johnson whether Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia is good for AMD or damaging to the broader ecosystem, Li declined to comment directly, citing it being her second day on the job.
  * She emphasized that a healthy, multi-chip ecosystem—spanning Nvidia, AMD, TPUs, and companies like Broadcom—alongside great labs, academia, and the public sector, benefits everyone.

## Spatial Intelligence, World Models & Products
* **Evolutionary Roots:** Li, who began laying the foundation for modern computer vision 20 years ago, noted that spatial intelligence—the loop between seeing, sensing, and interacting—is more than 540 million years old, dating back to ancient underwater animals.
* **World Models Defined:** World models connect pixels, 3D worlds, and 4D worlds with deep reasoning, generation, and understanding capabilities, moving AI beyond language.
* **Product Releases & Users:**
  * **Marble & Atlas:** World Labs released its first model, *Marble*, last year, and launched *Atlas*—a more advanced version of Marble—last week.
  * **Early Adopters:** Current users include avant-garde game designers, VFX artists, independent studios, architects, and robotics companies.
* **Market Opportunity:** Beyond established industries like VFX, gaming, design, and movies, Li sees world models transforming healthcare, education, manufacturing, and agriculture, with the market cap for robotics being "truly unbounded."
* **Competition:** Asked how World Labs differentiates from spatial intelligence efforts by Jeff Bezos (Prometheus) and Yann LeCun (AMI), Li expressed respect for both leaders but stated she has no insight into their work.

## The Public Sector Compute Crisis
* **Priced Out:** Having recently stepped down as co-director of the Stanford Human-Centered AI Institute (HAI), Li warned that universities and the public sector are not keeping up with commercial AI because they are "priced out" of tokens and compute.
* **10-Year Advocacy:** Li has advocated for public-sector AI resourcing for roughly 10 years, warning it would be "one of the biggest failures of our time" if open democratic societies fail to fund researchers, students, and educators.
  * Public-sector compute is essential for discovering cures for cancer, teaching the next generation, and maintaining an independent voice for benchmarking and accountability.

## AI Governance & Global Robotics Competition
* **Science-Based Policy:** Li, who co-authored a paper on world model governance this summer, urged Washington D.C. to adopt a balanced, pragmatic, and science-based (rather than science-fiction-based) governance framework.
